1.title: Risk, Issues and Impediments
1.text: Welcome to Module 11. This is the second Business Environment module. It covers what might happen, what has happened, and what is blocking the team. In Part 1, we plan risk management, identify risks and analyze them. Part 2 covers risk responses, reserves and monitoring. Part 3 covers issues and impediments, and what to do when a risk occurs. The central idea of the module is the line between a risk and an issue.

1.title: Where This Module Sits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits. The Business Environment domain has eight tasks, and this module covers two. Task five: plan and manage risk, from identifying risks to quantifying contingency and executing the risk plan. Task four: remove impediments and manage issues, including recognizing when a risk becomes an issue. The line between a risk and an issue is one of the most tested ideas on the exam. A risk that has occurred is an issue: log it, run the planned response and update the register.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Write risk statements, and set appetite, thresholds and scales. Identify and analyze risks, qualitatively and quantitatively. Choose response strategies and size reserves. Monitor risks, and tell risks, issues, impediments and change requests apart. Evaluate, prioritize and resolve impediments, and escalate correctly. And recognize when a risk becomes an issue.

1.title: Case Check-In: Risks on the Microgrid
1.text: Our microgrid has risks of several kinds. A threat: because the utility reviews interconnection slowly, approval may arrive late, delaying commissioning. An opportunity: if a battery price drops, the budget may fall, creating savings. Resident opposition: because Eastgate fears noise, they may object, delaying permits and causing rework. And overall risk: many small uncertainties together could push the whole project beyond its thresholds. Notice that each statement has a cause, an event and a consequence.

1.title: Risk: Key Terms
1.text: Key terms. A risk is an uncertain event or condition that, if it occurs, has a positive or negative effect on objectives. A threat is a risk with a negative effect, and an opportunity has a positive one. An issue is a current condition that has already occurred or is occurring. Overall risk is the effect of uncertainty on the project as a whole. Risk appetite is the uncertainty accepted for a reward, and a threshold is the measurable acceptable variation. Exposure is the aggregate impact of all risks. And resilience is the ability to absorb impacts and recover quickly.

1.title: Threats and Opportunities
1.text: Risk is not only bad news. A threat is a risk with a negative effect on objectives, such as delay, cost overrun or reputation damage. An opportunity is a risk with a positive effect, such as market share, cost savings or a positive environmental impact. The goal of the domain is to increase the probability and impact of positive risks, and decrease the probability and impact of negative risks, building resilience and reducing uncertainty. Positive risks deserve active responses: exploit, enhance or share them.

1.title: Writing a Risk Statement
1.text: Write each risk as cause, event, consequence. A register entry that says late deliveries is not a risk statement. A proper one says: because the utility reviews interconnection slowly, approval may arrive late, and commissioning is then delayed and cost rises. This separates the risk from its cause and its effect. It also helps separate real risks from concerns, issues and assumptions, because the event is uncertain and in the future.

1.title: Known and Unknown
1.text: PMBOK 8 classifies what is known and unknown. Known-knowns are facts and requirements, managed as part of scope: not a risk. Known-unknowns are the classic risks: there is knowledge to identify probability and impact, so use the risk register, a response strategy and a contingency reserve. Unknown-unknowns are emergent risks: handle them with management reserve and resilience, the ability to absorb and recover. Unknown-knowns are hidden facts: surface them through experts, lessons learned, historical information and stakeholders.

1.title: Appetite, Threshold and Exposure
1.text: Risk appetite is the degree of uncertainty an organization or individual will accept in anticipation of a reward. A risk threshold turns appetite into a measurable acceptable variation around an objective. For example, plus or minus five percent on cost means a lower appetite than plus or minus ten percent. Risk exposure is the aggregate measure of the potential impact of all risks at a point in time. Overall risk is the effect of uncertainty on the project as a whole. If it is too high, the organization may cancel the project.

1.title: The Six Risk Processes
1.text: Six risk processes. Four are in Planning. Plan Risk Management produces the risk management plan. Identify Risks produces the risk register and risk report. Perform Risk Analysis does qualitative analysis, and quantitative analysis when needed. Plan Risk Responses develops strategies, owners and reserves. In Executing, Implement Risk Responses carries out the agreed responses. In Monitoring and Controlling, Monitor Risks tracks risks, responses and effectiveness, and assigns owners. Identification and analysis repeat at the start of each phase or iteration.

1.title: Plan Risk Management
1.text: The risk management plan begins when the project is conceived and is completed early. It defines the risk strategy, the methodology, and roles and responsibilities. It covers funding, including protocols for contingency and management reserves, and timing. It covers risk categories, often a risk breakdown structure. And it records stakeholder risk appetite as measurable thresholds, with probability and impact definitions. Not everything fits the scales: ethical, reputation and morale risks need judgment alongside the numbers. Use the project's own scales and thresholds.

1.title: Risk Breakdown Structure
1.text: A risk breakdown structure groups sources of risk. In the PMBOK 8 example, level zero is all sources of project risk, and level one has four categories: technical, management, commercial and external. Technical covers scope definition, requirements and technology. Management covers resourcing, communication and planning. Commercial covers contract terms and suppliers. External covers legislation, exchange rates and the environment or weather. Categorizing risks shows where exposure concentrates, and supports generic responses to groups of risks.

1.title: Probability and Impact Scales
1.text: Each project defines its own probability and impact scales, typically five levels for a detailed approach, three for a simple one. Here is an example. Very high: over seventy percent probability, over six months, over five million dollars. High: fifty-one to seventy percent, three to six months, one to five million. Medium: thirty-one to fifty percent. Low: eleven to thirty percent. Very low: one to ten percent. The same scales evaluate threats and opportunities. Each project sets its own numbers.

1.title: Identify Risks
1.text: Identify risks iteratively: not all can be found at the start, so repeat at the start of each phase or iteration. Separate real risks from concerns, issues and assumptions, and include opportunities. Techniques: brainstorming, interviews and facilitation. Checklists from lessons learned, which are never exhaustive. Prompt lists such as PESTLE, TECOP and VUCA. SWOT, which adds internal risks. Assumption and constraint analysis, root cause analysis, and document analysis. AI and data analytics can broaden identification, with security and ethics checks.

1.title: The Risk Register and Risk Report
1.text: The risk register is created at identification and updated by every later process. Always record a unique identifier, a description in cause, event and effect form, a potential risk owner and potential responses. Optional data includes a title, category, status, causes and effects, risk triggers, the affected work and timing. A trigger is an event or condition showing that a risk is about to occur. The risk report gives sources of overall risk, plus a summary of individual risks, and communicates risk status to stakeholders.

1.title: Qualitative Analysis
1.text: Qualitative analysis evaluates each individual risk for probability and impact, using the plan's definitions. Score equals probability times impact, and thresholds for high, medium and low come from the plan. Threats and opportunities share one matrix. Stakeholders may perceive differences. Explore them and record the assumptions. Low-scoring risks go on a watch list. Risk categorization, by source, by work area, by phase or by root cause, shows where exposure concentrates. Qualitative analysis is done throughout the project.

1.title: Quantitative Analysis
1.text: Quantitative analysis numerically analyzes the combined effect of individual risks and other uncertainty on overall objectives, and it is used only when the project needs it. Simulation, such as Monte Carlo, models combined effects and gives, for example, the probability of finishing by a target date. Sensitivity analysis shows which risks matter most, displayed as a tornado diagram. Decision tree analysis calculates the expected monetary value of each branch to pick the best path. Influence diagrams show causal influences and relationships.

1.title: Expected Monetary Value
1.text: Expected monetary value equals probability times impact value. Threats are negative and opportunities are positive. For a decision, add the values along each branch, including the cost of the response, and choose the better, higher, expected value. In our example, buying protection costs twenty thousand and leaves a ten percent chance of a hundred thousand loss, which is ten thousand: a total of minus thirty thousand. Not buying leaves a forty percent chance of the same loss: minus forty thousand. Buy protection. Do not pay fifty thousand to remove a thirty thousand exposure.

1.title: Risk Planning and Analysis Traps: What PMI Expects
1.text: The traps so far. A risk that has occurred is an issue. Every risk needs an active owner. Use the project's own scales and thresholds, and do not invent ratings. Positive risks deserve active responses. Do qualitative analysis first, and quantitative only when needed. Risk management is continuous, so a register last updated at kickoff, or reviewed only at gates in an agile project, is the wrong answer. And do not confuse risk with issue, assumption, constraint or concern.

1.title: Part 1 Recap
1.text: Let us recap Part 1. A risk statement has a cause, an event and a consequence. Facts are not risks, and known-unknowns get contingency. The plan turns appetite into measurable thresholds and uses the project's own scales. Identification is iterative, for real risks only, with owners in the register. Qualitative analysis multiplies probability by impact and keeps a watch list. Quantitative analysis uses simulation, sensitivity analysis and decision trees with expected monetary value. In Part 2, we turn to responses and monitoring.

2.title: Plan Risk Responses
2.text: Part 2 covers responses. Plan Risk Responses develops options, selects strategies, agrees actions, assigns owners, and allocates resources and reserves. Responses must be timely, cost-effective, realistic and agreed by the parties involved. Early action is usually more effective than repairing damage later. Responses often need change requests, and response activities go into the plans and baselines. Compare the cost of a response with the expected monetary value of the risk. Do not pay fifty thousand to remove a thirty thousand exposure.

2.title: Response Strategies
2.text: For threats: avoid reduces probability to zero or isolates the objectives. Mitigate reduces probability or impact. Transfer shifts the impact and ownership of the response, through insurance, performance bonds, warranties or agreements, usually for a risk premium. Accept can be active, with a contingency reserve, or passive, with periodic review. For opportunities: exploit makes it certain, enhance raises probability or impact, share gives ownership to the party best able to capture it, and accept takes it if it happens. Escalate applies to both, when the risk is outside the project's scope or authority.

2.title: Escalating a Risk
2.text: Escalate a risk when it is outside the project's scope or beyond the project manager's authority. It is then managed at program, portfolio or organization level. The receiving party must accept ownership, and the project team does not monitor it further, though it may stay in the register for information. Use the defined escalation path, and bring facts, options and a recommendation. Do not escalate before analysis. And escalate only what is beyond scope or authority.

2.title: Terms the Exam Still Uses
2.text: Several terms are not in PMBOK 8 as strategy names, but the exam uses them. Residual risk is what remains after a response is implemented, and you keep reporting it. A secondary risk is a new risk created by a response. A fallback plan is used if the primary response proves ineffective. A workaround is an unplanned response to a threat that has occurred. A contingent response runs only if a defined trigger happens. Transfer is not elimination: insurance moves the financial impact, but the risk may remain.

2.title: Responses to Overall Project Risk
2.text: Overall project risk uses the same ideas applied to the whole project. Avoid: remove high-risk scope, and in the extreme case cancel the project. Exploit: add high-benefit scope or adjust thresholds. Transfer or share: a joint venture, subcontracting or a shared business structure. Mitigate or enhance: replan, change scope or priority, or reallocate resources. Accept: an overall contingency reserve. If overall risk is too high, the organization may cancel the project.

2.title: Reserves
2.text: Contingency reserve covers known risks with active response strategies, the known-unknowns. It sits in the schedule or cost baseline, and is released per the protocols in the risk management plan. It can be sized by a percentage, a fixed amount or quantitative analysis. Management reserve covers unforeseen work within scope, the unknown-unknowns. It is in addition to the baseline, never part of the cost baseline, and is usually released by senior management. Reserve analysis compares remaining risk with remaining reserve. A reserve burning faster than progress is a governance signal.

2.title: Quantifying Contingency
2.text: To quantify contingency, assess the risks, then size the reserve from expected monetary values or simulation. As an example from exam practice, risks with expected values of thirty, twenty and twenty thousand suggest a contingency of about seventy thousand, adjusted for dependencies and confidence. Identify contingency clearly in the cost documentation, and do not hide it in estimates. Reduce or release it as risks pass. Reserve analysis asks whether the reserve is sufficient for the remaining risk. Small and government projects often hold larger buffers.

2.title: Implement Risk Responses
2.text: In Executing, risk owners carry out the agreed responses as planned, and the project manager influences and supports them. Tools are influencing, the project information system and interpersonal skills. Outputs include change requests, and updates to the risk register, the risk report, the issue log, the lessons learned register and team assignments. If a response does not work, use the fallback plan or re-plan. Secondary risks go into the register. And a response that changes a baseline goes through change control. Fallback plan and secondary risk are exam practice terms. PMBOK 8 does not use them.

2.title: Monitor Risks
2.text: Monitor Risks tracks identified risks, the implementation of responses, new risks and the effectiveness of responses, and keeps every risk owned. Risk reviews reassess existing risks and find new ones, on a regular cadence. A risk audit examines the effectiveness of the risk management process, not individual risks. Reserve analysis asks whether reserves are still enough. Technical performance analysis compares technical achievement with plan, and deviations can signal threats or opportunities. A risk that occurs becomes an issue. Risks that can no longer occur are closed.

2.title: Security, Sustainability and AI Risks
2.text: The ECO gives three example areas. Security: a poor IT security risk stays in the register with an owner and a response that reduces exposure, such as patching, controls or replacing the weak component. Insurance transfers financial loss but does not protect the data. Sustainability: risks arise when cost is prioritized over stewardship, community impact is ignored, or regulation is underestimated. AI: ethical risks of bias, privacy and accountability, so a human reviews AI output. Compliance threats are risks until they occur.

2.title: Case Check-In: Risk Handling on the Microgrid
2.text: On the microgrid, each risk has an owner and a response. The permit delay is owned by the project manager: mitigate by early submission, with a trigger of no reply within two weeks. The battery lead time is owned by the procurement lead: transfer part of it through supplier terms, with reserve analysis each month. The battery price drop is an opportunity owned by the sponsor: enhance it through flexible ordering. And software risks sit in the backlog, reviewed at the start and end of each iteration.

2.title: Risk in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
2.text: Risk looks different by approach. Predictive: a formal plan, risk breakdown structure and scales up front, and workshops at planning and gates. A register and report go to the steering committee, with contingency and management reserves, and quantitative analysis on large work. Agile: lightweight planning, and risk identification at the start of each iteration by the whole team. Risks sit in the backlog, with short feedback loops and a risk review at the end of each iteration. Hybrid: a register for fixed elements and the backlog for iterative ones.

2.title: Risk Response Traps: What PMI Expects
2.text: The traps for responses and monitoring. Contingency covers known risks, and management reserve covers unknown unknowns and is not the project manager's to spend unilaterally. Compare the cost of a response with the risk's expected value. Transfer is not elimination. Escalate only what is beyond scope or authority, and after a valid escalation, ownership moves. Reporting a response is not closing a risk: report effectiveness and residual risk. In agile work, make risks visible in the backlog. And use change control when a response changes the baseline.

2.title: Issues and Impediments: Key Terms
2.text: Now issues and impediments. Key terms. An impediment is an obstacle that prevents the team from achieving its objectives. Examples are a waiting approval, missing access or data, a broken environment, an unavailable expert, or an unclear decision. An issue is a current condition that has already occurred and may need management attention. The issue log records and monitors issues. The impediment list is a visual chart showing description, severity and actions being taken. A risk trigger shows a risk is about to occur. And a workaround is temporary: the cause remains. The term workaround is exam practice wording, not PMBOK 8.

2.title: Risk, Issue, Impediment and Change Request
2.text: Tell them apart. A risk is future and uncertain, recorded in the risk register, with a planned response. Wording: might, could. An issue is present: it has occurred, recorded in the issue log, with analysis, decision and action. Wording: has now, was announced. An impediment is present and blocking the team, on the impediment list, to remove, work around or escalate. Wording: blocked, waiting for. A change request is a proposal to modify a baseline, in the change log, to assess and approve, defer or reject.

2.title: Key Relationships
2.text: Some key relationships. An issue can arise from a poorly managed risk, but it can also appear with no risk behind it. An impediment is an issue seen from the team's work: something that stops or slows the flow. A change request is one way to resolve an issue when a baseline or document must change. A conflict between people that disrupts the work is an issue to resolve. A false assumption, a missed dependency or a failed test can also create an issue. And read the issue log and the risk register together: they can reveal challenges tied to individual stakeholders.

2.title: Part 2 Recap
2.text: Let us recap Part 2. For threats: avoid, transfer, mitigate or accept. For opportunities: exploit, share, enhance or accept. Escalate only what is beyond scope or authority, and the receiver owns it. Contingency covers known risks, and management reserve covers unforeseen work. Risk owners run responses, with fallback plans for failures, and secondary risks go into the register. Monitoring means reviews, audits, reserve analysis and closing risks. Security, sustainability and AI risks have their own treatment. And we compared risks, issues, impediments and change requests. In Part 3, we manage issues and impediments.

3.title: The Management Loop
3.text: The management loop has six steps, matching the ECO enablers. Capture and log: this is the entry point, including recognizing a risk that has become an issue. Evaluate the impact. Prioritize and highlight. Choose and apply an intervention strategy, collaborating with stakeholders. Reassess continually, so impediments are being addressed. Close and learn, feeding the lessons learned register. Give every item one named owner, one action and one date.

3.title: Who Removes Impediments
3.text: Three levels remove impediments. The team self-organizes and removes the impediments within its reach, and raises the rest at once, for example at the daily coordination meeting. The project manager or scrum master, as a servant leader, removes what the team cannot. That means working with outside groups, negotiating and replanning. It means shielding the team from outside disruption, and escalating. The sponsor, customer, product owner and governance act on matters beyond the project management team's authority: decisions, funding, priorities, policy.

3.title: Evaluate the Impact
3.text: Understand before you act. Establish what is blocked, for whom, for how long and what happens if nothing changes. Look at eight dimensions. Schedule: is the critical path or iteration goal affected? Cost: idle time, rework, penalties. Scope and quality. Resources: who is waiting, and the morale. Risk: does it raise or create risks? Stakeholders and benefits. Compliance and safety exposure. And reach and control: one team or several, inside the team's control or not, recurring or not. Find the cause with root cause analysis.

3.title: Problem Solving and Root Cause
3.text: PMBOK 8's problem-solving method: define the problem, identify the root cause, generate possible solutions, choose the best, implement it, and verify that it worked. Tools are root cause analysis and the cause-and-effect diagram, and the five whys is a common exam-practice way to drill down. When several fixes have already failed, do not repeat the same repair and do not halt everything. Assess the impact and agree a different intervention strategy: work around it, replace the component, or reprioritize. Record the evaluation in the issue log.

3.title: Prioritize and Highlight
3.text: Rank open items by impact on the objectives and urgency, and work the highest first. As exam practice, an impact and urgency grid helps: high impact and urgent, remove now. High impact but not urgent, plan and own. Low impact but urgent, a quick fix or batch. Low impact and not urgent, watch. Give every item one named owner and limit how many are worked at once. Keep an impediment list where the team and stakeholders can see it, make it the first item at the daily coordination meeting, and report key issues upward. Report honestly: no green status while the team is blocked.

3.title: Intervention Strategies
3.text: Match the strategy to the cause and the impact. Remove the cause when it is within your control. Work with the owning group when the cause sits elsewhere, especially if it recurs. Negotiate or influence when priorities compete. Re-plan or re-sequence to work on unblocked items. Raise a change request when a baseline must change. Escalate when beyond your authority or persistent. Use a temporary workaround, keeping the item open. Add capacity or skills for a shortage. Accept and adjust when impact is low. And prevent recurrence by changing the process.

3.title: Apply and Reassess
3.text: Apply the strategy. Assign an owner, an action and a date, and make sure the owner can act. Tell the team and affected stakeholders what is being done and when to expect relief. Then reassess, because impediments move. A blocker can be cleared on paper and still slow the team, or shift into a new form. Ask the team whether it is gone. If the same impediment keeps returning, treat it as systemic: analyze it together, change the process, and update process assets. Close only when work flows.

3.title: When a Risk Becomes an Issue
3.text: You notice a risk has become an issue when a stated event has happened, a trigger has fired, or monitoring shows it. Then: confirm the facts. Log it in the issue log with an owner, action and date. Implement the planned response, using the reserves defined in the plan. Update the risk register and report: record that the risk occurred. Do not just raise the probability to one hundred percent, and do not add a duplicate. Check knock-on effects, including secondary and residual risks, and raise change requests. Inform stakeholders, escalate what is beyond your authority, and capture the lesson. Residual risk is an exam practice term for what remains after a response.

3.title: Related Situations
3.text: Related situations. If no response was planned, an unforeseen event arrives as an issue. Evaluate the impact. Collaborate on a resolution. Act, perhaps with a workaround. Then update the register for any new risks it reveals. A risk that never occurs, or whose window has passed, is closed in the register. It does not become an issue. A register last updated at kickoff is stale: set a regular review cadence. Once a valid escalation is accepted, ownership moves. And if a response needs more than the contingency reserve, follow the governance route for more funding.

3.title: Collaborate With Stakeholders to Resolve Issues
3.text: Collaborate with stakeholders. Identify the right people: who is affected, who owns the cause, who has authority, who can help. Bring them together when several are affected, especially when each proposes a different fix, and agree one approach. Do not simply adopt the proposal of the most affected party, the highest-ranking person or the owner of the cause. Use a structured approach, with facilitation, negotiation and conflict management. Decide at the right level. Record decisions, owners and dates, and communicate. With external parties, act within the agreement, and send contract changes through change control.

3.title: Escalating an Issue
3.text: Escalate when the matter is beyond your authority, or the cause sits outside the project. Escalate when it persists after reasonable attempts, or is severe and time-critical. And escalate when a compliance, safety or ethical threat is involved. Use the defined path and thresholds. Bring the facts and impact, what was tried, the options with their impacts, your recommendation, and the decision needed and by when. Agree who owns the matter afterwards. Do not escalate before analysis, skip levels without cause, hide a blocked item from the sponsor, or escalate and walk away. An escalated issue stays in the log until work flows.

3.title: The Issue Log and Impediment List
3.text: Know the records. The issue log records and monitors issues. It is an output of Manage Project Execution, and an input to closing. The impediment list is a visual chart of description, severity and actions, on the team board. The change log records change requests and decisions. The risk register is updated when a risk occurs. The lessons learned register captures lessons. A typical issue entry has an identifier, a description, and the impact and priority. It has an owner, actions and a due date. And it has a status and links. At closure, anything still open needs a formal decision and a named owner.

3.title: Case Check-In: An Impediment on the Microgrid
3.text: On our microgrid, the dashboard developers are waiting for controller interface details from the engineers. That is an impediment. Evaluate the impact: the iteration goal is at risk. Intervene: agree a standing review slot with the engineers, and work on unblocked items meanwhile. Reassess by asking the team whether work flows. If it recurs, treat it as systemic: run a cross-team retrospective, name one owner and change the working agreement. If it persists, take it to Elena Vasquez with facts, options and a recommendation.

3.title: Issues in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
3.text: Issues look different by approach. Predictive: issues go in the issue log and are reviewed at status meetings. The project manager removes them with the item's owner, with escalation to governance. Priority comes from baselines, the critical path and risk. Agile: captured in the daily meeting and the impediment list. Removed by the team first, then the scrum master or project manager. And prioritized by the iteration goal and flow. A risk that occurs becomes an impediment or backlog item. Hybrid mixes both, with the baseline envelope first.

3.title: Issue and Impediment Traps: What PMI Expects
3.text: The traps for issues and impediments. A risk that occurs is an issue: log it, run the response, update the register. Impediments get removed, not just logged, and recurring ones need action. Evaluate before acting, and find the root cause. Prioritize by impact and urgency, with one owner each. Reassess from the team's side, and treat repeats as systemic. Escalate with facts and options, by the defined path. And do not stop all work, repeat the same fix, or assign blame.

3.title: Module Recap
3.text: Let us recap the whole module. Risk: cause, event and consequence, with owners and the project's own scales. Responses: strategies, escalation, reserves and fallback plans. Monitoring: reviews, audits and reserve analysis, with a live register. Issues and impediments: evaluate, prioritize, intervene and reassess. And the line that matters most: a risk that occurs becomes an issue. Now it is time to test yourself. Five questions follow. For each one, pause the video, choose your answer, and then listen to the explanation.

3.title: Practice Question 1
3.text: Question one. A permit authority announces a three-month backlog. The project risk register lists this as a risk with a planned response. What should the project manager do now? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. A risk that has occurred is an issue, so it is logged, the planned response is executed, and the register is updated. Raising the probability, adding a duplicate risk, or waiting leaves the occurred event unmanaged.

3.title: Practice Question 2
3.text: Question two. The owner of an important risk has left the project, and the risk register has not been reviewed for two months. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. Every risk needs an active owner, and the register must be kept alive, so a new owner is assigned and the response is confirmed. Re-scoring, archiving, or pushing every risk to the sponsor does not fix ownership or cadence.

3.title: Practice Question 3
3.text: Question three. A threat could cost 30,000 dollars if it occurs, and a vendor offers to remove it for 50,000 dollars. What is the best action? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. A response costing more than the risk's exposure is usually not worth buying, so the threat is accepted actively with a contingency reserve. Paying more than the exposure, handing it to the sponsor, or ignoring it all skip a proportionate response.

3.title: Practice Question 4
3.text: Question four. A team waits every week for the same approval from a central group, and the project manager has so far only logged the delay each time. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. A recurring impediment caused by another group needs action with that group to remove the cause, not another log entry or a permanent workaround. Planning around it, adding capacity, or escalating before any attempt do not fix the recurring cause.

3.title: Practice Question 5
3.text: Question five. Three stakeholders propose three different fixes for a serious issue that affects all of them. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. When several stakeholders are affected and each proposes a different fix, the project manager brings them together and agrees one approach with a structured method. Following seniority, the most affected party, or the team's preference leaves others unheard.

3.title: Answers at a Glance
3.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: B. A risk that occurs becomes an issue to log, respond to and update. Question two: D. Assign a new owner, confirm the response and keep the register alive. Question three: A. A response costing more than the exposure is not worth buying. Question four: C. A recurring blocker needs action with the owning group. Question five: B. Bring the affected stakeholders together and agree one approach. That completes Module 11. Next, Module 12 covers change control, continuous improvement, organizational change and the external environment. See you there.
